summary: Considers what IPv6 support cellular hosts need on GPRS, UMTS and EPS networks, given the limits of cellular links in bandwidth, cost and delay. It is guidance for implementers.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 7066 guides people implementing IPv6 for cellular hosts on GPRS, UMTS, and EPS networks. It explains which existing IPv6 features apply and how cellular link behavior changes their use.

questions: does a cellular host need duplicate address detection
subtitle: Implementation guidance for IPv6 hosts connected through 3GPP cellular networks.

tldr.problem: IPv6 has many features, while cellular links have bandwidth, cost, and delay characteristics that call for specific host guidance.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 7066 explains which IPv6 node requirements apply to hosts on GPRS, UMTS, and EPS networks, including Neighbor Discovery, address configuration, DHCPv6, and router options.
tldr.outcome: This Informational guidance obsoletes RFC 3316. It complements the IPv6 Node Requirements and does not define a new protocol.

sections.title: Scope and Audience
sections.content:
This document focuses on cellular hosts that attach to GPRS, UMTS, or EPS networks. It complements the IPv6 Node Requirements in RFC 6434 where cellular links need clarification, and it is aimed mainly at implementers.

The document is Informational. It is not intended to replace or contradict IPv6 standards. Transition mechanisms are outside its scope, and the text treats IP-layer mobility as not relevant for most cases because movement is handled by link-layer mechanisms.
sections.plainLanguage: This is guidance for people who build cellular hosts. It explains how existing IPv6 rules apply to the cellular links named in the RFC.

sections.title: Neighbor Discovery on Cellular Links
sections.content:
GPRS, UMTS, and EPS links resemble point-to-point links. A host's neighbor on the cellular link is its default router, which it learns through Router Discovery. The link has no link-layer addresses, so address resolution and next-hop determination are not needed.

The host must support Neighbor Solicitation, Neighbor Advertisement, and Neighbor Unreachability Detection. The RFC recommends using confirmations from upper-layer protocols, such as TCP responses, DNS replies, RTCP feedback, and SIP responses, to reduce extra periodic signaling.
sections.plainLanguage: The cellular link connects the host to its default router without link-layer addresses. Replies from applications can also show that a remote endpoint is reachable.

sections.title: Address Configuration and DHCPv6
sections.content:
Stateless Address Autoconfiguration (SLAAC) is the only mandatory IPv6 address-configuration method for a 3GPP cellular host. Router Advertisements carry at most one prefix information option, with infinite valid and preferred lifetimes. The prefix is /64 and cannot be used for on-link determination.

The gateway supplies the interface identifier used for the host's link-local address, so the host does not need Duplicate Address Detection on the cellular interface. As of 3GPP Release-11, DHCPv6 is neither required nor supported for address autoconfiguration, although it may serve other configuration needs.
sections.plainLanguage: The cellular network supplies the prefix and interface identifier used to form the host's IPv6 address. DHCPv6 is not the method for configuring that address in the releases covered here.

sections.title: Additional Router and Configuration Options
sections.content:
The RFC recommends support for Default Router Preferences and More-Specific Routes, DNS configuration options in Router Advertisements, and the Prefix Exclude Option for DHCPv6 Prefix Delegation. These options can help hosts that also have other interfaces or need to configure downstream links.

A cellular host should honor the MTU option in Router Advertisements. The packet core uses tunneling, so the gateway may advertise an MTU that accounts for the extra overhead.
sections.plainLanguage: Several optional settings help a host use other interfaces, configure downstream networks, and choose packet sizes. The advertised MTU can account for tunneling inside the cellular network.

sections.title: Security and Privacy Considerations
sections.content:
IPsec is a fundamental part of IPv6 but is not mandatory. The host must follow the specified handling for overlapping fragments and must not fragment Neighbor Discovery messages. The RFC says it defines no new protocol or functionality and introduces no new vulnerabilities.

The security discussion notes that cellular airtime is costly and capacity is limited, so denial-of-service traffic can have greater effects. Local interfaces such as WLAN or Bluetooth should use access control to prevent others from using the host as an intermediary.
sections.plainLanguage: Cellular links have limited capacity, so extra traffic can disrupt service. Hosts should also control access through their local network interfaces.
